source.title: LLM Jailbreaks Exploit Attention Sinks
source.authors: Jonah Mackey; Stephen Zhang; Vardan Papyan

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether suffix-based jailbreaks suppress refusal-direction alignment using attention-sink modulation, rather than applying the original difference-in-means direction ablation or addition.
record.gate_note: The study cites prior results defining and causally validating the refusal direction, but does not repeat those tests. The ASR results in Table 2 compare attacks with suffix controls; they do not measure refusal-direction suppression and are not recorded as rows. The study reports sink counts and sink-modulation outcomes relevant to the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study does not ablate the difference-in-means direction. It uses that direction, computed as in Arditi et al., as a readout. It shows that amplifying attention sinks induced by adversarial suffixes lowers residual-stream alignment with the direction, which bears on V3's claim that attacks work by suppressing it. Only r6–r9 measure the direction. The ASR rows measure sink effects on attack success and do not show suppression of the direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that adversarial suffixes induce attention sinks and that modulating these sinks shifts ASR in both directions. They also conclude that amplifying the sinks suppresses residual-stream alignment with the Arditi et al. refusal direction. They read the sinks as a structural mechanism jailbreaks exploit.
record.recipe_differences: The study detects and modulates suffix-sink contributions in attention-head outputs, then measures alignment with a refusal direction computed following Arditi et al. It does not derive, ablate, or add the original difference-in-means direction.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies with sink gain λ and the sink threshold ϵ; the largest effects occur when relatively few sink positions are modulated. The authors also report smaller effects for a random-position control.

fits_no_version.finding: Modulating attention-sink positions in adversarial suffixes shifts jailbreak ASR monotonically: up to +176% under amplification and −84% under attenuation. The effect is 4–8× larger than for randomly chosen positions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention sinks induced by suffix-based jailbreaks causally contribute to attack success.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial suffixes induce more attention sinks per head than fluent, permuted, or random controls. Sinks per head correlate with ASR on all four models (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suffix-based jailbreaks show elevated suffix attention-sink prevalence, and sink prevalence correlates with attack success.

record.code_released: Code to reproduce all experiments and figures will be released upon publication.
record.peer_reviewed: preprint (under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027)
record.problems: The evaluation is limited to open-weight safety-aligned models in the 7–9B range and suffix-based, single-turn attacks. The study does not directly intervene on the refusal direction or assess general capabilities. Some per-condition results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text, and code is not yet released.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Training against refusal-direction ablation for robustness is not tested. The study never compares refusal alignment under the unmodified attack with harmful prompts without a suffix. No suppression is measured under sink attenuation, and no other attack families are tested.
No derivation of the direction is validated, and no ablation, addition, or capability check is run.

missing.what: The full λ sweep shows suppression of refusal alignment is graded in sink gain. The same trend holds when averaging over all response tokens.

record.verdict_notes: The link to the direction is shown only under artificial amplification (λ=10) of sinks already present in the attack. The study does not compare refusal alignment between the attack and a no-suffix condition, and does not measure alignment under attenuation. Refusal-direction validity is taken from Arditi et al. and not rechecked. Preprint under review.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not derive a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, ablate or add that direction, or test whether other abilities remain intact.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The study tests suffix-based attacks and sink modulation, not training against refusal-direction ablation or resulting robustness.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, conic, or multidirectional refusal representation.
No separate harmfulness judgment and refusal-decision representations are tested.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of the refusal direction is tested.
No comparison of refusal training methods or stages is made.

rows.subject: four safety-aligned models (aggregate: Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5-7B)
rows.operation_detail: Amplified the attention-head output contribution from detected suffix sinks by sweeping sink gain λ.
rows.value: Across all four models and both attack methods, ASR increased with amplification and decreased with attenuation; the trend was monotonic in λ.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals across suffixes are shown in Figure 4; numeric intervals not stated in text.
rows.note: The paper reports the trend across all models and both attacks as an aggregate; it does not give the individual plotted ASR values in the text.
rows.check: ASR under sink-gain modulation measures whether sinks drive attack success, not refusal-direction suppression. It does not bear on V3 as worded. Record under fits_no_version.

relationships.reason: Sink amplification erased roughly 80% of refusal-direction alignment at peak (r6, r9). This is consistent with suffix tokens acting by suppressing the direction.

relation.reason: Section 5 reports its own measurements of how suffix-sink contributions change alignment with the refusal direction. That bears directly on V3.

tranche.reason: It uses a different method on the same question: sink-subspace modulation, read out by cosine with an Arditi-style direction. The result bears on whether suffix attacks act by suppressing the direction.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] ids for the verdicts, so l1 and l2 follow the pack's order. The record says code=y, but the paper says code will be released upon publication. The year is blank: this is an ICLR 2027 submission. Section 5 / Figure 7 does not say which attack (GCG or PGD) was used. It also gives no uncertainty, and never measures refusal alignment under attenuation or for the attack against no suffix. The ICLR reviewer footer (line 144) is addressed to human reviewers, not an AI reader.

statements.correction: Section 5.2 / Figure 7: cosine of the first-response-token residual stream with an Arditi-style refusal direction, λ=10 vs λ=1 (no intervention). Peak suppression is about 80% in Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. Attack type not stated. No uncertainty reported for Figure 7. Code not yet released (to come on publication). Uncertainty is given for ASR (±SD in Table 2, bootstrap 95% CIs in Figure 4).
statements.problem: 80%, λ=10 and the two models are right. But Section 5.2 and Figure 7 never say the suffixes are GCG. 'With code' is wrong: code 'will be released upon publication'. The uncertainty is on ASR results only, not on the refusal-alignment result.

statements.correction: Across all four models, amplifying sinks (λ=10) lowers refusal alignment across layers. Peak suppression: about 80% for Llama-3-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, about 45% for Llama-3.1-8B, smaller for Gemma-2-9B (no number given). Gemma ASR: GCG 55.2%, PGD 71.0% (Table 2). Qwen also has high ASR (56.9%, 64.5%) and about 80% suppression.
statements.problem: 45% (Llama-3.1-8B) and the smaller, unquantified Gemma-2-9B reduction are right, measured at peak, at λ=10, on the first response token. But the authors report suppression in all four models. Tying Gemma's smaller drop to its high ASR is the synthesis's own inference. The study never measures how much the unmodified attack suppresses the direction, so it doesn't show attacks working unevenly.

statements.correction: Peak suppression at λ=10 vs λ=1, first response token: about 80% for Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, about 45% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, smaller (no number) for Gemma-2-9B-it.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but in this study the 80% vs 45% contrast is between Llama-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, which are the same family. So the factor here is model version, not model family. The values are peak-layer, at λ=10, on the first response token.
